notes: TRAP for any re-reader: this file contains TWO Mexican grants, and the one bound at the FRONT is the wrong one. Transcript pages 9-19 are expediente No. 541, 'Ano de 1845 ... ampliacion', an entirely separate PIO PICO grant of 23 Jan. 1846 for the vacant surplus lying between Encinitos and the rancho of Lorenzo Soto ('Angeles Enero 23 de 1846 ... declaro al Ciudadano Andres Ybarra dueno de todo el terreno baldio que resulte entre los linderos del terreno que posee y los de el rancho de Lorenzo Soto ... Pio Pico', stamped p.11; title stamped p.12). The original 1842 ALVARADO grant on which the claim actually rests sits much later, at stamped pp.20-21 (Spanish) and pp.22-24 (translation), as an exhibit to Santiago Arguello's deposition. An agent who read only pages 1-19 would have graded year ERR (1846) and governor ERR (Pio Pico) - both wrong. The register is right: the confirmed claim is the 1842 Alvarado league, and the Commission decree confirms 'one square league' only, consistent with the register's 4,431.03 patent acres. Also documented here: a genuine translator's error ('trece'/13th July rendered 'third of July', stamped p.23) that propagated into the claimant's petition (stamped p.4) and the Commission opinion (stamped p.26). Judicial possession was given 22 July 1842 by Justice of the Peace Jose Antonio Gongora (stamped pp.24-25), and the surveyors measured only half the league - the ground of the U.S. objection, overruled at stamped p.42. notes: A rare Indian grant that survived the Land Commission, and the register's era/year/governor are all correct. The half-sitio (media legua en cuadro) at El Escorpion was granted to three San Fernando neophytes on the strength of Fray Blas Ordaz's report of their 'buenos servicios' (stamped p.10); the Departmental Assembly approved it 26 May 1846 (stamped pp.13, 18, committee report signed S. Arguello). Juan Manso's deposition (stamped pp.6-7) is worth flagging for the ethnohistory: he was lessee of the San Fernando mission lands 1846-1852 and testified that Urbano had a house, vineyard, cattle and horses on the place, that Manuel was reputed to be Urbano's son, aged 24-26, and that 'the occupancy of Urbano has always been respected.' Note the petition (stamped p.4) shows a fourth party, Joaquin Romero, who took a one-fourth conventional-fee interest by conveyances of 26 July 1849 and 26 Sept. 1852; he is named alongside the three Indians in the District Court decree. Register's outcome 'Confirmed' is right and, unusually, the file proves finality all the way to a Supreme Court dismissal. Patent (claimed Dec. 11, 1876, GLO 409) is not in the file, but the 1876 mandate makes that date plausible; Phase C should check GLO. Hoffman 1862 agrees with the register on every field including the same abbreviated grantee string.

notes: METHOD WARNING for this chunk: I nearly graded outcome UV here. The file's own index of District Court papers (stamped pp.66-67) lists the transcript items and the 'Additional evidence' but does NOT list the decree, and the file's last leaves (stamped 65-77) are exhibits, not a judgment. The decree is buried mid-file at stamped pp.49-50. Reading only head + tail would have produced a wrong UV. This is one of the 'General Title' cases: Micheltorena, too busy in Dec. 1844 to draw individual titles for the Sacramento Valley petitioners, issued one blanket instrument and authorised Sutter to hand certified copies to those who had petitioned with his favourable informe. The Commission rejected on two grounds (only copies filed, no originals in evidence; and Neal had never petitioned the Governor before 22 Dec. 1844, so was not among the designated grantees). Both were then destroyed by new evidence taken in the District Court: John Bidwell recanted his Commission testimony on 3 July 1855, explaining 'I presented the petition of Neal to the Governor myself, and can only account for the error in consequence of being deaf in my left ear, and may have misunderstood the question' (index summary, stamped p.67), and the ORIGINAL Spanish petition to Micheltorena, on properly habilitado sello cuarto paper signed by Pablo de la Guerra, was produced as Exhibit No. 1 W.H.C. (stamped pp.73-74). Bidwell's second deposition of 30 Oct. 1855 authenticated the papers as genuine and identified the general title as in Sutter's own hand (stamped pp.45-46). Bidwell also testified that Micheltorena 'was personally acquainted with Samuel Neal ... and had a high personal regard for him. He was a blacksmith by trade and was a very useful man during the war which occurred in 1844.' Patent (claimed Apl. 4, 1860, GLO 14, 22,193.78 acres = 5 leagues) is not in the file, but the 1859 survey order makes it plausible; Phase C should check GLO and should also settle whether the patent issued under the name Esquon.

notes: IDENTITY WARNING: this is NOT the Los Angeles Los Feliz (which is SD 133, also in this chunk). This Feliz rancho is on the San Francisco peninsula, one square league in what was then San Francisco County and is now San Mateo County, bounded by the Sierra, the Cumbre de las Auras, San Pedro, Buriburi, San Mateo, the Arroyo de las Juntas and the Canada de Raymundo (stamped pp.19, 21, 78). Two ranchos, two grantees (Maria Ignacia Berdugo vs Domingo Feliz), two governors' years - easy to conflate in a register. The Commission's docket name 'Buriburi' is affirmatively WRONG and the file says so: witness William D. Harrington testified 'The Rancho called Buriburi lies on the East of the San Andreas and adjoins it. The San Andreas or Juntas separates the land of said Feliz from the Rancho of Buriburi' (stamped p.13). The Mexican expediente gives this tract no proper name at all, only 'el parage que demuestra el diseno respectivo' (stamped p.21), which is why the U.S. records had to invent one. Miramontes testified Feliz moved onto the land in 1844, built a wooden house ten varas by five, then an adobe, and ran about fifty head of cattle and fifteen horses (stamped pp.16-17). The survey was contested: the United States excepted that it 'extends too far southerly' and that squatters Patrick Cahill, Stephen Trowell and Michael Dolan claimed the southern portion by preemption (stamped pp.81-82), and the owners of the Canada de Raymundo grant objected too (stamped p.83) - which is why nine years pass between the 1855 decree and the 1864 decree approving the survey, and why the patent (claimed June 21, 1873, GLO 167) is so late. Spence also explains the compound name: 'The Rancho called "Guadalupe" and mentioned in this will as containing a little more than six leagues is made up of four separate grants called "Guadalupe", "Llano de los Correos", "Sanjones" and "Chualar" all of which tracts lie together and constitute the Rancho called "Guadalupe"' - only the first two are in this case. corrections.grantee: Andres and Jose Manuel, neophyte Indians of Mission San Luis Rey. Verbatim from the grant, stamped p.10: 'los Indigenas de la Mision de Sn. Luis Rey Andres y Jose Manuel.' Solme and Catarina are Jose Manuel's heirs, who joined Andres as U.S.-era claimants after Jose Manuel's death about 1850; they were never grantees.

notes: SECOND INSTANCE OF THE DOMINANT ERROR CLASS IN THIS CHUNK, and again the register departed from Hoffman to introduce it: Hoffman's 1862 table prints 'Andres and Jose Manuel', which is correct. As with rancho-guadalupe-llanitos-correos, the register's grantee string is identical to its own patent_to string ('Andres, Solme, and Catarina'), so the mechanism looks the same - the patentee list copied left into the grantee column. WARNING for anyone correcting this: the case file itself CONTRADICTS ITSELF on who Solme and Catarina were. The petition (stamped p.4) and the Commission opinion (stamped p.18) say Catarina was Jose Manuel's widow and Solme his mother; the deposition of Bacitis Valdez (stamped p.8) and the District Court opinion (stamped p.54) say Solme was the wife and Catarina the sister ('he left his Wife Salme and his sister Catarina as his heirs'). Do not assert either relationship as fact. This is a rare surviving Indian grant - a half sitio and its spring, granted to two San Luis Rey neophytes who were already living on and cultivating the land ('que hace tiempo ocupan y cultivan'), bordering the land of another Indian, Felipe. Valdez testified they had work oxen, cows, horses and mules, a house, a garden and fruit trees (stamped p.8). QUANTITY TRAP: the grant gives 'media legua en cuadro' but the alcalde measured a full league, and the Commission noted that the sworn translation's 'a half league square' means a quarter of a square league while the Spanish means a half (stamped p.19). Both courts confirmed HALF A SQUARE LEAGUE, consistent with the register's 2,219.41 patent acres. Patent (claimed Sept. 7, 1871, GLO 519) is not in the file; Phase C should check GLO.

notes: USE THIS RECORD AS THE CONTROL for the two grantee ERRs in this chunk. Here the grantee and the claimant are DIFFERENT people and the register got the distinction right: Jose Maria Orosco received the grant in 1845 and sold the rancho by public act on 5 Feb. 1847 to George W. Hamley, who was the U.S.-era claimant (petition stamped p.4; District Court opinion stamped p.68, 'a conveyance from said Orosio by deed to the present claimant'). The register puts Orosio in grantee and 'George W. Hamley' in patent_to, which is the correct assignment - so the register's data model is capable of holding the distinction, and rancho-guadalupe-llanitos-correos and rancho-guajome are lapses, not a systematic design flaw. Three sitios de ganado mayor about twelve leagues from Mission San Luis Rey, bounded by the Mesa de Pamo, the Potreros de Pauma and the sierra; reported vacant by Juan Maria Marron for the mission (17 Aug. 1845, stamped p.12) and by Sub-Prefect Santiago Arguello for the partido (28 Aug. 1845, stamped p.13); Departmental Assembly approval 3 June 1846 on the report of the Comision de Terrenos Baldios (stamped p.16). J. J. Warner testified that Orosco and his brother-in-law Jose Maria Alvarado lived on it in 1845 with a house, horses, brood mares and about five hundred head of cattle, and had 25 acres in barley and wheat (stamped pp.7, 69). The claimant's own surname is unstable in the file - HANLEY on the red label, HAMLEY on the transcript title and Surveyor General's certificate, HAMBLY in the Commission docket and the Attorney General's letter - so Phase C should not treat any one of these as authoritative when matching the GLO patent (claimed May 24, 1866, GLO 515). Patent not in the file.
